deep.reconstruction:
Context (§67–68, previous page): water flows from a large, constantly full reservoir (cross-section ff, height a) through a vertical cylindrical tube BC (section gg, length b) into a second vertical tube CD (section hh, length c), and out through an orifice kk. Euler's friction law makes the pressure decay along a tube of 'width' g with a factor e^{-αx/g}. He writes 𝔄=e^{-αa/f}, A=(1-𝔄)/α (and similarly 𝔅, B, ℭ, C), 𝔤=k⁴/g⁴, 𝔥=k⁴/h⁴. The efflux head is v = [A𝔅ℭ f + Bℭ g + C h − (1−𝔄𝔅ℭ) l] / [1 − (1−𝔅)ℭ𝔤 − (1−ℭ)𝔥]. As α→0 we have A f→a, B g→b and C h→c, so v→a+b+c. This is Torricelli's result for the total height AD.

This page (§69–71) argues as follows.
(i) If g=h, the case reduces to Case I, a single tube. If g>f effectively, BC is just part of the reservoir. So the genuinely new phenomena require BC much narrower than both neighbours.
(ii) Experiments show that a narrow middle passage markedly reduces the efflux velocity. In the frictionless theory the section gg does not enter v at all, so Euler ascribes the reduction to friction.
(iii) §70: when BC is much narrower, the jet already contracts before entering BC (vena contracta). On entering the wider CD it stays contracted for some distance. The effective conduit therefore has the shape βBBCCγ, with the upper vessel and lower tube partly 'narrowed'. Euler models this by an effective-length correction: increase the length b of the narrow tube by some amount and subtract corresponding amounts from a and c.
(iv) §71: b, a, c are henceforth effective lengths, with b larger and a, c smaller than measured. The correction to b grows as g/f and g/h decrease. On the next page this means that even a vanishing physical length (a thin orifice plate) receives a finite effective b, so b/g is large and 𝔅≈0.

This prepares the asymptotic analysis of a reservoir drained through a small hole into a lower tube. It also prepares the continuity (non-negative pressure) check at CC in §73.
errors: Physically, the dominant loss in flow through a narrow passage into a wider tube is the sudden-expansion (Borda–Carnot) loss of kinetic energy, not wall friction. Euler attributes the experimentally observed reduction 'aperte frictioni', which is an incorrect diagnosis by later standards. His friction law (decay ∝ e^{-αx/g}) is itself only a phenomenological assumption.

The effective-length correction (lengthen b, shorten a and c by 'tantumdem') is introduced ad hoc. Its magnitude is not derived, and it is not clear that equal amounts are subtracted from a and c. It is a fitting device rather than a deduction.

The claim that, without friction, gg would not affect the efflux holds only within steady one-dimensional Bernoulli theory with continuous flow. Euler himself notes in §73 that continuity (positive pressure) can fail.

ideas.what: Frictionless efflux head through a compound vertical tube equals the total height a+b+c, independent of the intermediate cross-sections
ideas.modern_name: Torricelli/Bernoulli efflux law for steady ideal flow
ideas.where_published: E260 and Euler's hydraulic papers of the 1750s (e.g. E258)

ideas.what: Contraction of the stream entering a narrow passage and persisting after entering a wider tube, so the effective conduit has a different shape
ideas.modern_name: vena contracta / flow separation at abrupt contraction and expansion

ideas.what: Representing entrance/exit contraction effects by lengthening the narrow tube in the friction calculation and shortening the adjacent sections
ideas.modern_name: equivalent-length method for minor losses (cf. end corrections)
ideas.usually_credited_to: 19th–20th c. hydraulic engineering practice (Darcy–Weisbach era); no single originator

missed.claim: Euler introduces an effective-length correction to absorb vena-contracta effects at a constriction into his friction calculation. The correction grows as the passage narrows relative to its neighbours, so even a zero-length orifice gets a finite effective length. This is an early qualitative form of the 'equivalent length' idea for minor losses, used here within a frictional (not energy-loss) framework. It is a modest historical precedent rather than a new mathematical result.
missed.quote: Quae circumstantia in calculum inducetur, si longitudo tubi gracilioris BC aliquanto maior aestimetur, quam reuera est; atque tantumdem de altitudine tuborum contiguorum dematur.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of minor interest to historians of hydraulics: an 18th-century precursor of equivalent-length modelling of fitting and orifice losses. No mathematical consequence for today.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is mostly physical motivation. The effective-length device for contraction effects is a mildly interesting precursor of the engineering 'equivalent length' notion. However, it is ad hoc, the physics (attributing losses to friction rather than expansion) is superseded, and E260 is a known if little-studied paper.
transcription_corrections: Transcription of this page is essentially accurate. One check on the neighbouring page: by the definition C=(1−ℭ)/α with ℭ=1−αc/h+α²c²/2h², one gets C = c/h − αcc/2hh. The '+' printed or transcribed on p.365 should be checked against the image.
